Repeated-measures mixed models

Source: vignettes/repeated-measures-lmm.Rmd
repeated-measures-lmm.Rmd

Repeated-measures fMRI analyses are often statistically simple but operationally awkward. You have one effect estimate per ROI or voxel, per subject, per visit or condition, and you want a group model that respects the repeated structure without hand-writing a loop over lmer() calls. fmrigds gives you a narrow, fast path for that case.

This vignette shows the supported contract: one grouping factor, Gaussian responses, shared observation layout across samples, and either a random intercept or a random intercept plus one within-subject slope. By the end, you will have one model-level GDS containing fixed-effect estimates and variance-component assays that you can inspect or write out like any other group result.

What does the input look like?

The easiest route is a stacked long table with one row per sample, subject, and repeated-measure level. Here we build a small ROI example with three visits:

subjects <- paste0("sub-", sprintf("%02d", 1:6))
visits <- c("pre", "mid", "post")
time <- c(-1, 0, 1)

rm_df <- expand.grid(
  sample = c("ROI_1", "ROI_2"),
  subject = subjects,
  contrast = visits,
  KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

subject_intercept <- c(-0.25, -0.10, 0.00, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30)
names(subject_intercept) <- subjects
subject_slope <- c(-0.05, -0.02, 0.00, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05)
names(subject_slope) <- subjects
sample_shift <- c(ROI_1 = 0.00, ROI_2 = 0.35)
sample_slope <- c(ROI_1 = 0.45, ROI_2 = 0.70)

rm_df$time <- time[match(rm_df$contrast, visits)]
rm_df$beta <- 0.9 +
  sample_shift[rm_df$sample] +
  subject_intercept[rm_df$subject] +
  (sample_slope[rm_df$sample] + subject_slope[rm_df$subject]) * rm_df$time
rm_df$var <- 0.04

knitr::kable(head(rm_df), row.names = FALSE)
sample subject contrast time beta var
ROI_1 sub-01 pre -1 0.25 0.04
ROI_2 sub-01 pre -1 0.35 0.04
ROI_1 sub-02 pre -1 0.37 0.04
ROI_2 sub-02 pre -1 0.47 0.04
ROI_1 sub-03 pre -1 0.45 0.04
ROI_2 sub-03 pre -1 0.55 0.04

The time column is constant within each visit, so it can be collapsed into contrast-level metadata during ingestion.

What is the fastest end-to-end path?

Use gds(..., contrast_data_cols = "time") to put the repeated-measure metadata on the contrast axis, then call reduce() with one of the restricted LMM reducers:

g_rm <- gds(rm_df, contrast_data_cols = "time") |>
  reduce(
    method = "lmm:ri_slope1",
    formula = ~ time,
    options = list(
      slope = "time",
      covariance = "diag",
      fit = "REML",
      theta_mode = "voxelwise"
    )
  ) |>
  compute()

The result is still a GDS, but the subject and contrast axes have collapsed to the model level. A compact summary is usually easier to read than printing individual assay arrays:

knitr::kable(lmm_summary_display, row.names = FALSE)
sample intercept time vc_intercept vc_slope lambda_slope
ROI_1 0.942 0.453 0.025 0.001 793553955
ROI_2 1.292 0.703 0.025 0.001 793766066

Fixed-effect outputs still follow the same naming convention as the regression reducers (coef:<term>, se_coef:<term>, t_coef:<term>, p_coef:<term>), while variance components are exposed as ordinary assays such as vc_intercept, vc_slope, and lambda_slope.

When should you use pooled vs voxelwise theta?

theta_mode = "pooled" estimates one shared variance structure across all samples. theta_mode = "voxelwise" estimates variance parameters separately for each sample. Pooled mode reuses one variance structure, so it is typically faster; voxelwise mode is more flexible.

g_pooled <- gds(rm_df, contrast_data_cols = "time") |>
  reduce(
    method = "lmm:ri_slope1",
    formula = ~ time,
    options = list(
      slope = "time",
      covariance = "diag",
      fit = "REML",
      theta_mode = "pooled"
    )
  ) |>
  compute()

theta_compare <- data.frame(
  sample = sample_labels(g_rm),
  pooled_lambda = round(as.numeric(assay(g_pooled, "lambda_slope")), 3),
  voxelwise_lambda = round(as.numeric(assay(g_rm, "lambda_slope")), 3),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(theta_compare, row.names = FALSE)
sample pooled_lambda voxelwise_lambda
ROI_1 792143154 793553955
ROI_2 792143154 793766066 
knitr::kable(transform(bench_times, elapsed = round(elapsed, 3)), row.names = FALSE)
theta_mode elapsed
pooled 0.028
voxelwise 1.460

What if your repeated-measure metadata is already separate?

If your time, visit order, or other repeated-measure annotations already live outside the long table, attach them explicitly with with_contrast_data().

contrast_df <- data.frame(time = time, row.names = visits)

g_attached <- gds(rm_df[c("sample", "subject", "contrast", "beta", "var")]) |>
  with_contrast_data(contrast_df) |>
  reduce(
    method = "lmm:ri_slope1",
    formula = ~ time,
    options = list(
      slope = "time",
      covariance = "diag",
      fit = "REML",
      theta_mode = "pooled"
    )
  ) |>
  compute()

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    sample = sample_labels(g_attached),
    time = round(as.numeric(assay(g_attached, "coef:time")), 3),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
sample time
ROI_1 0.453
ROI_2 0.703

If you only need a random intercept, use method = "lmm:ri" instead:

g_ri <- gds(rm_df, contrast_data_cols = "time") |>
  reduce(
    method = "lmm:ri",
    formula = ~ time,
    options = list(fit = "REML", theta_mode = "pooled")
  ) |>
  compute()

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    sample = sample_labels(g_ri),
    time = round(as.numeric(assay(g_ri, "coef:time")), 3),
    lambda = round(as.numeric(assay(g_ri, "lambda")), 3),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
sample time lambda
ROI_1 0.453 34.765
ROI_2 0.703 34.765

What is supported, and what is intentionally out of scope?

The repeated-measures LMM reducers are deliberately narrower than lmer():

  • one grouping factor only
  • Gaussian outcomes only
  • shared observation layout across all samples
  • random intercept only ("lmm:ri") or random intercept plus one slope ("lmm:ri_slope1")
  • no crossed random effects
  • no general random-effects formula grammar

That restriction is the point: it lets fmrigds reuse one design across many responses and produce a whole-brain or whole-ROI result with one call to reduce().

Where do you go next?

  • See ?reduce for the reducer contract and options.
  • See ?with_contrast_data if your repeated-measure metadata is already separate from the long table.
  • See inst/examples/fmrigds_lmm_benchmark.R for a benchmark harness that compares pooled and voxelwise theta modes.
